title: Refit a car's ratcheting fuel cap: start it square in a recessed neck, turn to the click, push the sprung door to latch
instruction: Put the fuel cap back on: start it square on the filler neck, turn it clockwise until it clicks, push the fuel door shut until it latches, let go.
context: Refitting the fuel cap is the last step of a fill-up on cars with a screw cap. The cap must be started square on a coarse thread at the back of a recessed pocket, its axis level, then turned about a third of a turn until the ratchet clicks; a cap left short of the click lets fuel vapour out. The door is then pushed shut against its spring, a little past flush, to its push latch. About 240 million people held a US driving licence in 2024 (FHWA), and 56% of drivers surveyed filled up at least once a week before 2020 (HONK survey, NACS Daily 2020). Refuelling is also a job: 92,530 US automotive and watercraft service attendants (O*NET 53-6031.00) in May 2023 (BLS OEWS), the job that fills tanks where self-service is not allowed. Sources in README.
setup: Metres; x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the ground; origin on the ground midway between the arm bases, which stand at (0, +/-0.305, 0.75) on a table cut back to a strip under them (x -0.19 to 0.14, y -0.65 to 0.65, top 0.7475); the station's own table is taken out. (1) Car, fixed: the right rear quarter of a parked Volkswagen Golf VII (2013 to 2015) (data: https://www.volkswagen-newsroom.com/en/vehicle-data-golf-7-profile-20039), its body side facing the arms: the side from the sill (0.20) to the roof (1.44), 1.66 long (y -1.30 to the tail at 0.36), with the rear wheel in its arch (centre y -0.184, 0.30 up; tyre 205/55 R16), the side window, the C-pillar and the rear lamp. Its face at the pocket is the plane x = 0.370, flat there and curving in towards the sill and above the belt line (0.98); its colliders are boxes 0.075 deep behind that face, from the sill to the belt line, y -0.60 to 0.22, leaving the pocket open. The flap's height, its size and the wheel's place were measured on a side photograph of a Golf VII, scaled by its 2,637 mm wheelbase. (2) Fuel pocket: a recess 238 mm wide x 145 mm tall in the face, centred y -0.030, z 0.870, its floor at x 0.438. (3) Filler neck: a 44 mm bore (52 mm outside) on a horizontal axis along x at y -0.010, z 0.870, its mouth at x 0.420 with a 4 mm flared lead-in. (4) Fuel door: a 232 x 140 x 3 mm plate, 150 g, on a vertical hinge at x 0.370, y -0.147 (the pocket's right edge, towards the car's front), standing open 90 degrees out towards the arms; a light spring (0.06 N m/rad, at most 0.2 N m) holds it open; its range is 3 degrees past open to 2 degrees past flush. From flush, its push latch's catch pushes back with up to 0.8 N m about the hinge (8 N at 10 cm from it, 3.4 N at the free edge); pushed 0.8 degrees past flush against it, the latch catches and holds the door flush. The cap's holder, a V cradle, stands 45 mm off the door's back, low, so that it sits under the fitted cap when the door is shut. (5) Fuel cap (the car's own screw cap, Volkswagen 5Q0201550A, https://oemwolf.com/oem-parts/5q0201550a.html; its retaining strap left out), free: a 67 mm x 20 mm shell with a raised grip bar 50 x 14 x 12 mm on its face and a 40 mm x 16 mm plug behind it, 80 g. It starts resting in the cradle, centred at (0.245, -0.118, 0.850), its axis along y, plug against the door, grip bar towards the arms' left. (6) Thread (code): it catches when the plug is 8 to 9 mm into the bore, its axis within 1.5 mm of the neck's and within 4 degrees of square. Then the cap's travel into the neck follows its own clockwise turn at 20 mm a turn (a multi-start thread), against a drag of 0.15 N m that rises to 1.5 N m over the last sixth of a turn; 6.5 to 7.5 mm (about a third of a turn) on, the shell seats on the neck's mouth and the ratchet clicks; turned further, it slips and turns back freely (running drag only). Backed off 0.8 mm past the catch, the cap is free again. Nothing is random. Real trial: a parked Golf VII, its right rear quarter beside the arms' table, the table's front edge 0.23 m from the body side, so that the pocket's centre is 0.37 m in front of the arm bases and 0.12 m above them.
scoring: Read at the end of the run; only the drop latches. 0: the cap falls below the pocket's lower edge (its centre under 0.77 m above the ground), or the thread not caught. 0.25: the thread caught and turned on at least 1 mm (about 18 degrees). 0.5: turned on at least a quarter turn (5 mm). 0.75: turned to the seat and the click (lost if turned back about 5 degrees). 1.0: clicked, the door latched and within 2 degrees of flush, and every part of both grippers 2 cm or more from the cap and the door with its cradle, held 3 s. Real trial: a cap that falls below the pocket's lower edge (on its strap or to the ground), judged from the video, scores 0. Measure the turn T from catch to click once; after each run turn the cap on by hand: it ratchets within 5 degrees, 0.75; the turn left is T minus 90 degrees or less, 0.5; T minus 18 degrees or less and the cap on the neck, 0.25. Latched, the flap stays flush when let go; flush, a straightedge. 1.0: latched, flush, and both hands visibly off the cap and flap for 3 s, from the video.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at setup's sizes; the cap is free until its thread catches. The thread, click and push latch are code: the cap's travel follows its own turn; the drag and click torques (0.15 and 1.5 N m) and the latch's 0.8 N m are estimates, not measured; a real ratchet may slip somewhat higher or lower. Check with a torque screwdriver or spring scale. Thread flanks do not collide; bore and lip do. Strap left out. The car's side is a visual mesh over box colliders, its curvature an estimate.
scores: Dream-1: 0.0 (1200 steps). Demo: 1.0 (both arms, 575 steps, 28.75 s, GPU). 2 N door push 0.75; door left open 0.75; turned back 30 deg 0.5; unturned 0; cap left in cradle 0; cap dropped 0; wrist at half the click torque 0.5; nothing 0.
